craft_claim: Classical rhetoric theorizes prose rhythm, euphony, and word-order as constitutive of sublimity, not as ornament added after the sense is fixed.

supporting_evidence.location: On the Sublime, sections on rhythm, euphony, and word-arrangement
supporting_evidence.note: Longinus treats the music of language — rhythm, sound, and the ordering of words — as one of the sources of the sublime.

supporting_evidence.location: On Literary Composition, on the melody of prose and the choice/arrangement of sounds
supporting_evidence.note: Dionysius devotes a systematic treatise to the 'music' of prose, analysing how the selection and ordering of sounds and rhythms produce effects distinct from the thought.
Horace's warning against a brilliant passage sewn in for display shows that classical theory treats sound/ornament as governed by the whole.

scope: Western rhetorical and literary tradition; applicable to any prose that aims at elevation through sound.
exceptions: Plain-style traditions (e.g., Attic restraint) that deliberately suppress rhythm as a value.
